```
PACMAN(8)                        Pacman Manual                       PACMAN(8)

NAME
       pacman - package manager utility

SYNOPSIS
       pacman <operation> [options] [targets]

DESCRIPTION
       Pacman is a package management utility that tracks installed packages
       on a Linux system. It features dependency support, package groups,
       install and uninstall scripts, and the ability to sync your local
       machine with a remote repository to automatically upgrade packages.
       Pacman packages are a zipped tar format.

       Since version 3.0.0, pacman has been the front-end to libalpm(3), the
       "Arch Linux Package Management" library. This library allows
       alternative front-ends to be written (for instance, a GUI front-end).

       Invoking pacman involves specifying an operation with any potential
       options and targets to operate on. A target is usually a package name,
       file name, URL, or a search string. Targets can be provided as command
       line arguments. Additionally, if stdin is not from a terminal and a
       single hyphen (-) is passed as an argument, targets will be read from
       stdin.

OPERATIONS
       -D, --database
           Operate on the package database. This operation allows you to
           modify certain attributes of the installed packages in pacman's
           database. It also allows you to check the databases for internal
           consistency. See Database Options below.

       -Q, --query
           Query the package database. This operation allows you to view
           installed packages and their files, as well as meta-information
           about individual packages (dependencies, conflicts, install date,
           build date, size). This can be run against the local package
           database or can be used on individual package files. In the first
           case, if no package names are provided in the command line, all
           installed packages will be queried. Additionally, various filters
           can be applied on the package list. See Query Options below.

       -R, --remove
           Remove package(s) from the system. Groups can also be specified to
           be removed, in which case every package in that group will be
           removed. Files belonging to the specified package will be deleted,
           and the database will be updated. Most configuration files will be
           saved with a .pacsave extension unless the --nosave option is used.
           See Remove Options below.

       -S, --sync
           Synchronize packages. Packages are installed directly from the
           remote repositories, including all dependencies required to run the
           packages. For example, pacman -S qt will download and install qt
           and all the packages it depends on. If a package name exists in
           more than one repository, the repository can be explicitly
           specified to clarify the package to install: pacman -S testing/qt.
           You can also specify version requirements: pacman -S "bash>=3.2".
           Quotes are needed, otherwise the shell interprets ">" as
           redirection to a file.

           In addition to packages, groups can be specified as well. For
           example, if gnome is a defined package group, then pacman -S gnome
           will provide a prompt allowing you to select which packages to
           install from a numbered list. The package selection is specified
           using a space- and/or comma-separated list of package numbers.
           Sequential packages may be selected by specifying the first and
           last package numbers separated by a hyphen (-). Excluding packages
           is achieved by prefixing a number or range of numbers with a caret
           (^).

           Packages that provide other packages are also handled. For example,
           pacman -S foo will first look for a foo package. If foo is not
           found, packages that provide the same functionality as foo will be
           searched for. If any package is found, it will be installed. A
           selection prompt is provided if multiple packages providing foo are
           found.

           You can also use pacman -Su to upgrade all packages that are
           out-of-date. See Sync Options below. When upgrading, pacman
           performs version comparison to determine which packages need
           upgrading. This behavior operates as follows:

               Alphanumeric:
                 1.0a < 1.0b < 1.0beta < 1.0p < 1.0pre < 1.0rc < 1.0 < 1.0.a < 1.0.1
               Numeric:
                 1 < 1.0 < 1.1 < 1.1.1 < 1.2 < 2.0 < 3.0.0

           Additionally, version strings can have an epoch value defined that
           will overrule any version comparison, unless the epoch values are
           equal. This is specified in an epoch:version-rel format. For
           example, 2:1.0-1 is always greater than 1:3.6-1.

       -T, --deptest
           Check dependencies; this is useful in scripts such as makepkg to
           check installed packages. This operation will check each dependency
           specified and return a list of dependencies that are not currently
           satisfied on the system. This operation accepts no other options.
           Example usage: pacman -T qt "bash>=3.2".

       -U, --upgrade
           Upgrade or add package(s) to the system and install the required
           dependencies from sync repositories. Either a URL or file path can
           be specified. This is a "remove-then-add" process. See Upgrade
           Options below; also see Handling Config Files for an explanation on
           how pacman takes care of configuration files.

       -F, --files
           Query the files database. This operation allows you to look for
           packages owning certain files or display files owned by certain
           packages. Only packages that are part of your sync databases are
           searched. See File Options below.

       -V, --version
           Display version and exit.

       -h, --help
           Display syntax for the given operation. If no operation was
           supplied, then the general syntax is shown.

OPTIONS
       -b, --dbpath <path>
           Specify an alternative database location (the default is
           /var/lib/pacman). This should not be used unless you know what you
           are doing.  NOTE: If specified, this is an absolute path, and the
           root path is not automatically prepended.

       -r, --root <path>
           Specify an alternative installation root (default is /). This
           should not be used as a way to install software into /usr/local
           instead of /usr.  NOTE: If database path or log file are not
           specified on either the command line or in pacman.conf(5), their
           default location will be inside this root path.  NOTE: This option
           is not suitable for performing operations on a mounted guest
           system. See --sysroot instead.

       -v, --verbose
           Output paths such as the Root, Conf File, DB Path, Cache Dirs, etc.

       --arch <arch>
           Specify an alternate architecture.

       --cachedir <dir>
           Specify an alternative package cache location (the default is
           /var/cache/pacman/pkg). Multiple cache directories can be
           specified, and they are tried in the order they are passed to
           pacman.  NOTE: This is an absolute path, and the root path is not
           automatically prepended. If DownloadUser is set in pacman.conf(5),
           then the specified user must have permission to access the cache
           directory.

       --color <when>
           Specify when to enable coloring. Valid options are always, never,
           or auto.  always forces colors on; never forces colors off; and
           auto only automatically enables colors when outputting onto a tty.

       --config <file>
           Specify an alternate configuration file.

       --debug
           Display debug messages. When reporting bugs, this option is
           recommended to be used.

       --gpgdir <dir>
           Specify a directory of files used by GnuPG to verify package
           signatures (the default is /etc/pacman.d/gnupg). This directory
           should contain two files: pubring.gpg and trustdb.gpg.  pubring.gpg
           holds the public keys of all packagers.  trustdb.gpg contains a
           so-called trust database, which specifies that the keys are
           authentic and trusted.  NOTE: This is an absolute path, and the
           root path is not automatically prepended.

       --hookdir <dir>
           Specify a alternative directory containing hook files (the default
           is /etc/pacman.d/hooks). Multiple hook directories can be specified
           with hooks in later directories taking precedence over hooks in
           earlier directories.  NOTE: This is an absolute path, and the root
           path is not automatically prepended.

       --logfile <file>
           Specify an alternate log file. This is an absolute path, regardless
           of the installation root setting.

       --noconfirm
           Bypass any and all "Are you sure?" messages. It's not a good idea
           to do this unless you want to run pacman from a script.

       --confirm
           Cancels the effects of a previous --noconfirm.

       --disable-download-timeout
           Disable defaults for low speed limit and timeout on downloads. Use
           this if you have issues downloading files with proxy and/or
           security gateway.

       --sysroot <dir>
           Specify an alternative system root. This path will be prepended to
           all other configuration directories and any repository servers
           beginning with file://. Any paths or URLs passed as targets will
           not be modified. This allows mounted guest systems to be properly
           operated on.

       --disable-sandbox
           Completely disables the sandbox applied to the process of
           downloading files on Linux systems. Equivalent to jointly
           specifying --disable-sandbox-filesystem and
           --disable-sandbox-syscalls.

       --disable-sandbox-filesystem
           Disable the filesystem restrictions part of the sandbox applied to
           the process downloading files on Linux systems. Useful if
           experiencing Landlock related failures while downloading files when
           running a Linux kernel that does not support this feature.

       --disable-sandbox-syscalls
           Disable the syscall filtering part of the sandbox applied to the
           process downloading files on Linux systems. Useful if experiencing
           seccomp related failures while downloading files when running a
           Linux kernel that does not support this feature.

TRANSACTION OPTIONS (APPLY TO -S, -R AND -U)
       -d, --nodeps
           Skips dependency version checks. Package names are still checked.
           Normally, pacman will always check a package's dependency fields to
           ensure that all dependencies are installed and there are no package
           conflicts in the system. Specify this option twice to skip all
           dependency checks.

       --assume-installed <package=version>
           Add a virtual package "package" with version "version" to the
           transaction to satisfy dependencies. This allows disabling the
           specific dependency checks without affecting all dependency checks.
           To disable all dependency checking, see the --nodeps option.

       --dbonly
           Adds/removes the database entry only, leaving all files in place.

       --noprogressbar
           Do not show a progress bar when downloading files. This can be
           useful for scripts that call pacman and capture the output.

       --noscriptlet
           If an install scriptlet exists, do not execute it. Do not use this
           unless you know what you are doing.

       -p, --print
           Only print the targets instead of performing the actual operation
           (sync, remove or upgrade). Use --print-format to specify how
           targets are displayed. The default format string is "%l", which
           displays URLs with -S, file names with -U, and pkgname-pkgver with
           -R.

       --print-format <format>
           Specify a printf-like format to control the output of the --print
           operation. The possible attributes are: "%a" for arch, "%b" for
           builddate, "%d" for description, "%e" for pkgbase, "%f" for
           filename, "%g" for base64 encoded PGP signature, "%h" for
           sha256sum, "%m" for md5sum, "%n" for pkgname, "%p" for packager,
           "%v" for pkgver, "%l" for location, "%r" for repository, "%s" for
           size, "%C" for checkdepends, "%D" for depends, "%G" for groups,
           "%H" for conflicts, "%L" for licenses, "%M" for makedepends, "%O"
           for optional depends, "%P" for provides and "%R" for replaces.
           Implies --print.

UPGRADE OPTIONS (APPLY TO -S AND -U)
       -w, --downloadonly
           Retrieve all packages from the server, but do not install/upgrade
           anything.

       --asdeps
           Install packages non-explicitly; in other words, fake their install
           reason to be installed as a dependency. This is useful for makepkg
           and other build-from-source tools that need to install dependencies
           before building the package.

       --asexplicit
           Install packages explicitly; in other words, fake their install
           reason to be explicitly installed. This is useful if you want to
           mark a dependency as explicitly installed so it will not be removed
           by the --recursive remove operation.

       --ignore <package>
           Directs pacman to ignore upgrades of package even if there is one
           available. Multiple packages can be specified by separating them
           with a comma.

       --ignoregroup <group>
           Directs pacman to ignore upgrades of all packages in group, even if
           there is one available. Multiple groups can be specified by
           separating them with a comma.

       --needed
           Do not reinstall the targets that are already up-to-date.

       --overwrite <glob>
           Bypass file conflict checks and overwrite conflicting files. If the
           package that is about to be installed contains files that are
           already installed and match glob, this option will cause all those
           files to be overwritten. Using --overwrite will not allow
           overwriting a directory with a file or installing packages with
           conflicting files and directories. Multiple patterns can be
           specified by separating them with a comma. May be specified
           multiple times. Patterns can be negated, such that files matching
           them will not be overwritten, by prefixing them with an exclamation
           mark. Subsequent matches will override previous ones. A leading
           literal exclamation mark or backslash needs to be escaped.

QUERY OPTIONS (APPLY TO -Q)
       -c, --changelog
           View the ChangeLog of a package if it exists.

       -d, --deps

           required by any installed package.

       -e, --explicit

           packages that are not required by any other package.

       -g, --groups
           Display all packages that are members of a named group. If a name
           is not specified, list all grouped packages.

       -i, --info
           Display information on a given package. The -p option can be used

           two --info or -i flags will also display the list of backup files
           and their modification states.

       -k, --check
           Check that all files owned by the given package(s) are present on

           contain the needed mtree file.

       -l, --list
           List all files owned by a given package. Multiple packages can be

       -m, --foreign
           Restrict or filter output to packages that were not found in the
           sync database(s). Typically these are packages that were downloaded
           manually and installed with --upgrade.

       -n, --native
           Restrict or filter output to packages that are found in the sync

       -o, --owns <file>
           Search for packages that own the specified file(s). The path can be
           relative or absolute, and one or more files can be specified.

       -p, --file
           Signifies that the package supplied on the command line is a file
           and not an entry in the database. The file will be decompressed and
           queried. This is useful in combination with --info and --list.

       -q, --quiet
           Show less information for certain query operations. This is useful
           when pacman's output is processed in a script. Search will only
           show package names and not version, group, and description
           information; owns will only show package names instead of "file is
           owned by pkg" messages; group will only show package names and omit

       -s, --search <regexp>
           Search each locally-installed package for names or descriptions
           that match regexp. When including multiple search terms, only
           packages with descriptions matching ALL of those terms are
           returned.

       -t, --unrequired
           Restrict or filter output to print only packages neither required
           nor optionally required by any currently installed package. Specify
           this option twice to include packages which are optionally, but not
           directly, required by another package.

       -u, --upgrades
           Restrict or filter output to packages that are out-of-date on the
           local system. Only package versions are used to find outdated
           packages; replacements are not checked here. This option works best
           if the sync database is refreshed using -Sy.

REMOVE OPTIONS (APPLY TO -R)
       -c, --cascade
           Remove all target packages, as well as all packages that depend on
           one or more target packages. This operation is recursive and must
           be used with care, since it can remove many potentially needed
           packages.

       -n, --nosave
           Instructs pacman to ignore file backup designations. Normally, when
           a file is removed from the system, the database is checked to see
           if the file should be renamed with a .pacsave extension.

       -s, --recursive
           Remove each target specified including all of their dependencies,
           provided that (A) they are not required by other packages; and (B)
           they were not explicitly installed by the user. This operation is
           recursive and analogous to a backwards --sync operation, and it
           helps keep a clean system without orphans. If you want to omit
           condition (B), pass this option twice.

       -u, --unneeded
           Removes targets that are not required by any other packages. This
           is mostly useful when removing a group without using the -c option,
           to avoid breaking any dependencies.

SYNC OPTIONS (APPLY TO -S)
       -c, --clean
           Remove packages that are no longer installed from the cache as well
           as currently unused sync databases to free up disk space. When
           pacman downloads packages, it saves them in a cache directory. In
           addition, databases are saved for every sync DB you download from
           and are not deleted even if they are removed from the configuration
           file pacman.conf(5). Use one --clean switch to only remove packages
           that are no longer installed; use two to remove all files from the
           cache. In both cases, you will have a yes or no option to remove
           packages and/or unused downloaded databases.

           If you use a network shared cache, see the CleanMethod option in
           pacman.conf(5).

       -g, --groups
           Display all the members for each package group specified. If no
           group names are provided, all groups will be listed; pass the flag
           twice to view all groups and their members.

       -i, --info
           Display information on a given sync database package. Passing two
           --info or -i flags will also display those packages in all
           repositories that depend on this package.

       -l, --list
           List all packages in the specified repositories. Multiple
           repositories can be specified on the command line.

       -q, --quiet
           Show less information for certain sync operations. This is useful
           when pacman's output is processed in a script. Search will only
           show package names and not repository, version, group, and
           description information; list will only show package names and omit
           databases and versions; group will only show package names and omit
           group names.

       -s, --search <regexp>
           This will search each package in the sync databases for names or
           descriptions that match regexp. When you include multiple search
           terms, only packages with descriptions matching ALL of those terms
           will be returned.

       -u, --sysupgrade
           Upgrades all packages that are out-of-date. Each
           currently-installed package will be examined and upgraded if a
           newer package exists. A report of all packages to upgrade will be
           presented, and the operation will not proceed without user
           confirmation. Dependencies are automatically resolved at this level
           and will be installed/upgraded if necessary.

           Pass this option twice to enable package downgrades; in this case,
           pacman will select sync packages whose versions do not match with
           the local versions. This can be useful when the user switches from
           a testing repository to a stable one.

           Additional targets can also be specified manually, so that -Su foo
           will do a system upgrade and install/upgrade the "foo" package in
           the same operation.

       -y, --refresh
           Download a fresh copy of the master package databases (repo.db)
           from the server(s) defined in pacman.conf(5). This should typically
           be used each time you use --sysupgrade or -u. Passing two --refresh
           or -y flags will force a refresh of all package databases, even if
           they appear to be up-to-date.

DATABASE OPTIONS (APPLY TO -D)
       --asdeps <package>
           Mark a package as non-explicitly installed; in other words, set
           their install reason to be installed as a dependency.

       --asexplicit <package>
           Mark a package as explicitly installed; in other words, set their
           install reason to be explicitly installed. This is useful if you
           want to keep a package installed even when it was initially
           installed as a dependency of another package.

       -k, --check
           Check the local package database is internally consistent. This
           will check all required files are present and that installed
           packages have the required dependencies, do not conflict and that
           multiple packages do not own the same file. Specifying this option
           twice will perform a check on the sync databases to ensure all
           specified dependencies are available.

       -q, --quiet
           Suppress messages on successful completion of database operations.

FILE OPTIONS (APPLY TO -F)
       -y, --refresh
           Download fresh package file databases (repo.files) from the server.
           Use twice to force a refresh even if databases are up to date.

       -l, --list
           List the files owned by the queried package.

       -x, --regex
           Interpret each query as a regular expression.

       -q, --quiet
           Show less information for certain file operations. This is useful
           when pacman's output is processed in a script, however, you may
           want to use --machinereadable instead.

       --machinereadable
           Print each match in a machine readable output format. The format is
           repository\0pkgname\0pkgver\0path\n with \0 being the NULL
           character and \n a linefeed.

HANDLING CONFIG FILES
       Pacman uses the same logic as rpm to determine action against files
       that are designated to be backed up. During an upgrade, three MD5
       hashes are used for each backup file to determine the required action:
       one for the original file installed, one for the new file that is about
       to be installed, and one for the actual file existing on the file
       system. After comparing these three hashes, the following scenarios can
       result:

       original=X, current=X, new=X
           All three files are the same, so overwrites are not an issue.
           Install the new file.

       original=X, current=X, new=Y
           The current file is the same as the original, but the new one
           differs. Since the user did not ever modify the file, and the new
           one may contain improvements or bug fixes, install the new file.

       original=X, current=Y, new=X
           Both package versions contain the exact same file, but the one on
           the file system has been modified. Leave the current file in place.

       original=X, current=Y, new=Y
           The new file is identical to the current file. Install the new
           file.

       original=X, current=Y, new=Z
           All three files are different, so install the new file with a
           .pacnew extension and warn the user. The user must then manually
           merge any necessary changes into the original file.

       original=NULL, current=Y, new=Z
           The package was not previously installed, and the file already
           exists on the file system. Install the new file with a .pacnew
           extension and warn the user. The user must then manually merge any
           necessary changes into the original file.

EXAMPLES
       pacman -Ss ne.hack
           Search for regexp "ne.hack" in package database.

       pacman -S gpm
           Download and install gpm including dependencies.

       pacman -U /home/user/ceofhack-0.6-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.gz
           Install ceofhack-0.6-1 package from a local file.

       pacman -Syu
           Update package list and upgrade all packages afterwards.

       pacman -Syu gpm
           Update package list, upgrade all packages, and then install gpm if
           it wasn't already installed.

CONFIGURATION
       See pacman.conf(5) for more details on configuring pacman using the
       pacman.conf file.

SEE ALSO
       alpm-hooks(5), libalpm(3), makepkg(8), pacman.conf(5)

       See the pacman website at https://archlinux.org/pacman/ for current
       information on pacman and its related tools.

BUGS
       Bugs? You must be kidding; there are no bugs in this software. But if
       we happen to be wrong, please report them to the issue tracker at
       https://gitlab.archlinux.org/pacman/pacman/-/issues with specific
       information such as your command-line, the nature of the bug, and even
       the package database if it helps.
```

   - Allow `systemctl [--user] <verb> *` for status, show, cat, is-active, is-enabled, is-failed, is-system-running, list-units, list-unit-files, list-timers, list-sockets, list-dependencies, list-jobs, show-environment and get-default, plus `rtk systemctl status *`. A remote option after the verb (`-H`, `--host`, `-M`, `--machine`) asks; before the verb, nothing matches, so it asks anyway.
   - Analyzer: accept show-environment and get-default as reads (fixes that false block), and skip options that take a value, so `systemctl -t service list-units` is no longer blocked.
   - `journalctl *`, with ask rules on the shortest prefixes of its maintenance/write flags: `--vacuum-*`, `--rotate`, `--flush`, `--sync`, `--synchronize-on-exit`, `--relinquish-var`, `--smart-relinquish-var`, `--setup-keys`, `--update-catalog` and `--cursor-file`, which writes a file. Analyzer: resolve abbreviated options; today `--rot` and `--vac=1d` slip through.
2. **Disks and network**
   - `lsblk *`, `findmnt *`, and exact `mount` and `mount -l`. The analyzer lets only those two forms through (fixes the bare `mount` false block); every other mount stays blocked.
   - ip, 32 rules: `ip a|addr|address|l|link|r|ro|route|n|neigh|neighbor|neighbour *`, plus `ip -br|-4|-6|-j a|addr|link|route|neigh *`.
   - The ip analyzer matches objects and verbs the way the iproute2 source does (abbreviated, in the same order: `ip link s` is set, `ip a s` is show). It blocks add, change, replace, delete, set, flush, prepend, append, test, restore and property, also `-batch` (`-b`), and `netns|vrf exec` when the command it runs writes.
3. **Packages**
   - `pacman -Q*` and `pacman --query *` (pacman refuses a second operation). Analyzer blocks `-R`, `-U`, `-S`/`-F` with y, u, c, w or install targets, and `-D --asdeps|--asexplicit`.
   - `flatpak list|info|remotes|ps *`; `snap list|info|connections|services *` and exact `snap version`. snap is not installed here, so its rules come from the docs only.
4. **Containers**
   - docker and podman: `ps|images|inspect|logs|top|port|diff|history|version|info *`, `image ls|inspect|history`, `container ls|inspect|logs|top|port|diff`, `volume|network ls|inspect`, `system df`, `stats --no-stream`; `context ls|show|inspect` (docker) and `pod ps|inspect` (podman); `rtk docker ps|images|logs *`.
   - Patterns always start with the subcommand. Docker rejects `-H`, `--context` and `--config` after it (tested), so those forms ask.
   - podman does accept its engine flags after the subcommand (tested). `--runtime`, `--conmon`, `--hooks-dir` and `--network-cmd-path` name programs it runs; `--root`, `--tmpdir` and similar create directories. Each gets an ask rule.
   - `--format` templates have no file or exec functions.
   - New `commands.json` write list for docker and podman; the analyzer blocks:
     - run, create, start, stop, restart and kill;
     - rm, rmi, cp and commit;
     - build, pull, push and tag;
     - load, import, login and logout;
     - every `prune`, and `volume|network create|rm`;
     - `context use|create|rm|update|import|export`;
     - save and export with `-o`, and podman's global `--out FILE`.

     exec, attach and the rest still ask.
5. **VMs**
   - `virsh [-c qemu:///system|qemu:///session] list|dominfo|domstate|domblklist|domiflist|net-list|pool-list|vol-list *`. Other connection URIs ask, because a URI like `qemu+ext://…?command=` runs a program.
   - Analyzer blocks a single string argument containing `;`: I tested `virsh -c test:///default 'list; destroy test'` and it destroyed the domain. It also blocks `-l`/`--log FILE`.
   - `VBoxManage list *` and `vagrant box list *`. I tested that `box list` does not evaluate the Vagrantfile; `vagrant validate` does.
6. **git**
   - `git grep*`; `-O` and `--op*` ask. Analyzer blocks `-O` inside a bundle (`-nOcmd`, which globs cannot see) and blocks a pager command that writes.
   - `git check-ignore*`, `git show-ref*`, `git for-each-ref*`.
   - `git hash-object*`: `-w` asks, and the analyzer blocks it in every form (including `-wt blob`).
7. **Exact `--version`:** node, bun, npm, git, gh, opencode, hk, docker, podman, VBoxManage, vagrant, chezmoi, flatpak and virsh. I ran each with an empty HOME: only gh (writes a device-id) and opencode (creates its log directory) write anything, and only their own state.
8. **docs:** CHANGELOG, README, CONTRIBUTING, TODO.

I will not touch `src/plugin.ts`, `inject.ts`, `tools.ts`, `index.ts` or `test/integration` (only if a rule test needs it). `insync` stays out.

Questions:
- Q1: Keep `python3 --version` out? It is harmless, but python3 is on your "never allow" list.
- Q2: Allow `gh --version` and `opencode --version`, even though they write their own state and log files?
- Q3: Are 32 ip rules OK, or only the 12 object-led ones? The option-led ones cover forms like `ip -br addr` from the log.
- Q4: A bundled `systemctl status -aH host` escapes the `-H` ask. It is a remote read, and libsystemd passes `--` before the host to ssh. Acceptable?
- Q5: Do the pacman write blocks belong in this PR, or allow `-Q` only?

## Assistant (Build · Claude Opus 5.5 · 45.1s)

_Thinking:_
This is a big PR, so I want to be systematic about it. I'm planning the commit order: systemd tooling first, then disks/networking, packages, containers, VMs, and finally git-related commands.

For systemd, I'm thinking through how to catch bundled or attached forms of `-H`/`--host` and `-M`/`--machine` so they can't bypass the remote-connection check — things like `-Hhost`, abbreviated long options like `--ho` or `--mach`, and bundled short flags. The glob-based analyzer can catch some attached forms but misses bundled ones, so I need to decide how strict to make the blocking rules for these remote-access flags.

I'm now extending this same remote-machine concern to journalctl, which also supports `-M`/`--machine` to query logs from a different container or host.

I decide to keep both systemctl and journalctl `-M` flagged for confirmation since both touch a separate manager/journal context, even though they're read-only operations. Now I'm moving on to implementing the analyzer changes, starting with a regex to classify read-only systemctl subcommands like status, show, cat, help, and list/is-prefixed commands.

I'm also cataloging the systemctl flags that take values—short ones like `-H`, `-M`, `-p`, `-P`, `-s`, `-n`, `-o`, and long ones like `--host`, `--machine`, `--type`, `--property`, `--job-mode`, `--signal`, and others—so the parser can correctly skip their arguments when scanning the command line.

I'm reasoning through edge cases where misparsing `--legend` as boolean versus required-argument could shift verb detection, but either interpretation still seems to land on blocking the command correctly, so the ambiguity doesn't actually break the safety check.

Now I'm moving to implementation: refactoring analyze.ts to extract a dedicated systemctlWrites function instead of inline conditionals, and doing the same for journalctl, starting with mapping out journalctl's dangerous long options like cursor-file, flush, relinquish-var, and rotate.

For the prefix-matching logic, since journalctl uses getopt_long (not getopt_long_only), I need the analyzer to treat unambiguous prefixes of long options as resolving to that option — so `--sync` is exact and safe to flag, but shorter prefixes like `--sy` or `--s` are ambiguous and should be blocked defensively since real behavior would error out anyway.

Still mapping unique prefixes...

Now I'm shifting to building the actual allow-list rules, writing failing tests first for the systemctl and journalctl analyzers. For systemctl I'm enumerating the read-only verbs (status, show, cat, is-active, is-enabled, etc.) and pairing each with both the bare and `--user` forms, which gets me to around 30 rules, while handling the no-argument commands like `show-environment` and `get-default` as exact matches plus their `--user` variants.

I'm also checking edge cases like `-H`/`--host`, `-M`/`--machine` flags and options like `--root=PATH` or `--image=PATH`, making sure these still match the wildcard patterns since they're read operations even when they touch remote hosts or disk images. I want to be careful that none of these supposedly read-only verbs actually carry hidden side effects.

I'm also realizing the rtk-prefixed forms need their own explicit patterns since the wildcard rules don't match when "rtk" precedes the systemctl command, so I'm adding separate ask-patterns for the rtk variants with -H and -M flags, plus extending the analyzer regex to cover docker ps/images/logs and systemctl status alongside the existing git/du/df/diff checks.

Now I'm ready to start writing out everything for the first commit, beginning with the tests.

## Assistant (Build · Claude Opus 5.5 · 21.5s)

_Thinking:_
I'm defining helper sets for systemctl's short and long options that require values, so I can correctly parse which flags need an argument following them.

I'm also writing a detection function for whether a systemctl invocation is a "write" command versus a safe read-only one, handling `--` separators, long option abbreviations like `--host`/`--machine`, and resolving ambiguous prefixes to know when to skip the next arg as a value. Simplifying for now since fully resolving all possible abbreviations would require the complete systemctl long-option list.

Even after a verb, getopt-style permutation means options and values can still appear later in the args, like "systemctl status -n 20 sshd", so the loop must keep scanning. The final decision is: if a verb exists and isn't in the read-only whitelist, flag it as changing system state; if no verb at all, treat it as listing units and allow it. For -H/-M bundling or abbreviation issues, the message should tell the user to pass -H HOST as a separate option instead. Now I'm moving on to building out the journalctl option lists, starting with the long-form flags pulled from its help text.

I'm defining journalctl's write-related options (like flush, rotate, vacuum variants) and writing a function that scans arguments for long-form flags, matching exact names or abbreviations against this write-blocking set, and returning a block message if a dangerous one is found. There are some edge cases where a value consumed by one option happens to look like another flag (e.g. a `-g` grep value that reads "--rotate"), which could cause harmless false positives in detection, but I'm treating those as acceptable tradeoffs.

Checking the edge cases around option matching confirms the logic holds - the "-4" and bare "-" cases resolve correctly without false matches against "-loops" or other flags.

But I spot a real bug: `-color=always` isn't properly handled, since my matches() function compares the full string including "=always" and fails to recognize it as the color flag. Real iproute2 specifically supports "-color" with an "=" suffix as a special case, so without handling that, a command like `ip -color=always addr add x` would slip through unblocked since the option parser would bail on "unknown option" rather than continuing to analyze the object. I need to special-case color matching by stripping anything after "=" before comparing against "-color", since no other option supports that syntax.

I should add a test for `ip -color=always addr add [redacted:ip]/24 dev eth0` being blocked, verify it fails first, then apply the fix.

Now I'm moving on to pacman, flatpak, and snap — working out how to detect the pacman operation from its flags, since it supports both short clusters and long options with getopt-style abbreviation matching that need careful disambiguation.

Now I'm working out write-vs-read determination per operation: remove and upgrade always write, while sync (S) is read-only if it has search/info/list/groups/print flags and no refresh/sysupgrade/clean/download flags, otherwise it writes. I'm continuing this logic for database (D) operations based on asdeps/asexplicit-type flags.

Query, files (F) with refresh, query/version/help are reads, and I'm now mapping which short-option letters consume a value (like dbpath and root) versus act as standalone flags, since that affects how clustered short options get parsed correctly.

Operation letters are the uppercase D Q R S T U F, with h for help staying lowercase. I'm sketching the parser logic: iterate through args, stop at "--", resolve long options by exact match or unique prefix against the full set, and map long operation names (database, query, remove, sync, deptest, upgrade, files) to their corresponding letters, plus mapping relevant long flags like refresh, sysupgrade, clean, search, info, list, groups, print formats, and asdeps/asexplicit to their short equivalents.

For short options, I handle the ones that take values (like -b or -r) by breaking out and skipping the next argument, while noting that letters are context-dependent -- -u means sysupgrade only in sync context, -c means clean/changelog/cascade depending on operation, -p means print or file depending on context, and so on. For abbreviation resolution on long names, I check for exact matches first, then unique prefixes, and if ambiguous I treat it conservatively since pacman would just error out anyway.

For operation detection, I check for the uppercase operation letters or their long forms, and if more than one operation is specified pacman errors with "only one operation may be used at a time," so that case can be treated as harmless. I'm also mapping out the block messages for each destructive operation (-S, -R, -U, -D, -F) and considering whether query-only invocations like -Q with various flags remain safe, since combining -Q with a second operation would also trigger that same error.

Sync queries like `-Ss foo` are reads too, but since the brief only asks for `-Q*`, I'll leave those out and move on to flatpak.

For flatpak I'd allow read-only subcommands like list, info, remotes, ps, and version, including options like `--file-access` or `--installation` that don't write anything—global flags before the subcommand just fall through to asking. For snap, similarly allow list, info, version, services, and connections since none of these mutate state, and I'm working through concrete pacman examples like `-Qqen` and `-Qi openssh` to confirm the pattern holds.

I'm sorting pacman commands into allow (query operations), ask (like `-Ss` or `-Si`), and block (sync, remove, install, database operations) categories, testing edge cases like combining `-Qi` with `-R` flags where pacman itself would reject multiple operations as an error, making it safe even if my analyzer's matching logic is a bit loose there.

```json
}
```

## Assistant (Build · Claude Opus 5.5 · 42.4s)

_Thinking:_
I'm mapping out virsh's global CLI options that appear before the actual command—things like connection URI, debug level, logging, and flags like quiet/readonly—since virsh relies on getopt_long and may allow abbreviated long options that I need to account for in the analyzer.

I'm also working through a tricky edge case: when a single remaining argument contains spaces but no semicolon, virsh parses it as a string command, but my tokenizer treats it differently, joining words before checking against the allowlist. I'm tracing through examples like `virsh 'destroy test'` versus `virsh 'list --all'` to verify whether the decide logic correctly blocks writes while still allowing safe read commands through.

The real danger is `virsh 'list; destroy test'`, where my logic might incorrectly allow a chained write command because the joined string happens to match the read pattern prefix. I'm concluding I should treat any single quoted argument containing a semicolon as suspicious by default — splitting it and checking each sub-command's verb against the set of allowed read verbs, and blocking the whole thing if any sub-command isn't a known-safe read operation.

I'll be conservative and only block when the args after options form exactly one string containing ";" or a newline, to avoid false positives on edge cases like quoted options.

Now I'm working out allow-list rules for VBoxManage, vagrant, and virsh — listing out which prefixes (like qemu:///system or qemu:///session contexts) paired with which read-only verbs (list, dominfo, domstate, etc.) should be permitted.

I'm also considering whether `virsh list` using the default URI is safe, reasoning that the default connection comes from user config the agent doesn't control, so that's fine. Time to move on to writing tests first.

```
# Changelog

All notable changes are documented here. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/)
and the project follows [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- Write guard for read-only agents (`plan`, `explore`, agents with `edit: deny`): blocks write redirections in any
  position, `tee` to files, file-modifying commands, `sed -i`, mutating git and package-manager commands and more,
  including behind wrappers and command substitutions.
- Shared, community-extensible rules in `rules/` (allowlist, always-ask flags, command classification, expected
  verdicts) with JSON Schemas.
- Event log of commands, blocks, prompts and answers for read-only agents.
- Reviewed learning: "always" answers become candidates; `/guard-review` and the `readonly_guard_review` /
  `readonly_guard_update` tools add vetted rules after an explicit confirmation of the exact pattern.
- `opencode-readonly-guard` command-line tool: `check`, `vet`, `rules`, `review`, `install`.
- Plugin options (`agents`, `allow`, `store`, `logDir`, `toast`, `command`).
- herdr rules: read-only `herdr` commands (`agent list`, `pane read`, `status`, …) are allowed in read-only agents;
  every other subcommand always asks and cannot be learned; `update`, `worktree create|remove`,
  `integration install|uninstall`, `session delete`, `plugin install|update`, `api schema --output` and `pane run` of a
  writing command are blocked.
- The `herdr-ui` preset: `herdr tab rename` and `herdr notification show`, which only change what herdr displays, are
  allowed when opencode runs in a herdr pane (`HERDR_ENV=1`) and not elsewhere. Switch it off with
  `"presets": { "herdr-ui": false }` in the plugin options, the store or herdr's own `readonly-guard.json` (in the
  directory of `HERDR_CONFIG_PATH`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/herdr`; read only inside herdr, never written, the last
  source wins); `allow` patterns from these sources pass the same safety check. UI commands listed by the user only
  take effect inside herdr. The `init` log event gains the `presets` in effect.
- Rules learned from real sessions: read-only agents no longer ask for text tools (`echo`, `printf`, `sort`, `uniq`,
  `cut`, `tr`, `comm`, `join`, `diff`, `basename`, `dirname`, `strings`), process and system reads (`date`, `du`,
  `df`, `pgrep`, `whoami`, `id`, `getent`, `printenv`, `env`, `command -v`, `hostname`), git reads (`ls-tree`,
  `rev-list`, `merge-base`, `worktree list`, `ls-remote`, `remote -v`, the listing forms of `branch` and `tag`, the
  reading forms of `config`), `npm view` and the mise reads (`--version`, `ls`, `ls-remote`, `tasks`, `settings`,
  `config ls|get`), with their `rtk` forms. Their write options ask (`sort --compress-program/-T`, `date -s`,
  `git ls-remote --upload-pack`, `npm view --cache/--logs-dir`, `mise -y`) and the write guard blocks
  `uniq IN OUT`, `date -s`/`date MMDDhhmm`, `hostname NAME`, `sort --compress-program=<writer>`,
  `git ls-remote --upload-pack=<writer>` and `mise set` / `npm set`.
- Exact `<program> <subcommand> --help` commands for git, herdr, npm and mise are allowed, after the always-ask flags
  (`git commit --help`, `herdr worktree create --help`); `opencode-readonly-guard rules` reports them.

### Fixed

- The write guard blocked a sole trailing `--help` (`herdr worktree create --help`, `npm install --help`) like the
  subcommand itself.
- The write guard missed writes: `git remote -v add|rename|remove`, `git branch -v|--sort|--format NAME` and
  `git tag --sort|--format NAME` (these flags do not list), abbreviated or bundled git branch and tag write options
  (`git branch -a --edit-desc`, `-rd`), `sort --out=FILE`, and `uniq - OUT` / `uniq IN 5`. It blocked
  `git tag -n1 NAME`, which lists.
- `/guard-review` proposed already allowed stages of compound commands: every candidate was offered the general
  patterns of all the stages, and the prompt statistics counted allowed commands. Only the stages the current rules
  still ask about count now, each with its own general pattern.

[Unreleased]: https://github.com/silopolis/opencode-readonly-guard/commits/main

```

**Commits:** the 8 planned ones in order, plus a 9th, `test(rules)`, that replaces your machine's unit and VM names in the test data. The new argument parsers are in a new module, `src/programs.ts`. Every analyzer change was written as a failing test first. The plugin files you named and `test/integration` are untouched.

**Your answers, applied:**
- **Q1:** `node --version` and `python3 --version` are allowed as exact commands only. `node -v`, `python3 -V` and anything with more arguments still ask (there are cases for this).
- **Q2:** `gh --version` and `opencode --version` are allowed; their rule reasons say they write their own state (gh a device id, opencode its log file). `mise version` does the same, and its reason says so too.
- **Q3:** all 32 ip rules are in. The ip tests cover every verb abbreviation (resolved in iproute2's own order: `ip link s` is set, `ip a s` is show), `-batch`/`-b`/`-ba`, `-color=always`, `netns add|attach|set|delete` and `netns|vrf exec`.
- **Q4:** `systemctl` with `-H` or `-M` inside a bundle, or abbreviated (`--ho=host`), is now blocked with "write -H HOST as a separate option so it asks".

**Things I confirmed by running the real programs:**
- `virsh 'list; destroy test'` destroyed the test domain: one quoted string runs every command in it, while the rules only see `virsh list`. The guard now blocks a single string containing `;` or a newline.

- Docker refuses `-H`, `--context` and `--config` after the subcommand, so allow rules that start with the subcommand never cover another daemon. Podman's `--remote`, `--connection` and `--url` behave the same.

**Other changes:**
- Fixed false blocks: bare `mount`, `systemctl show-environment` and `get-default`, and `systemctl -t service list-units`. Abbreviated journalctl maintenance options such as `--rot` and `--vac=1d` used to slip through and are now blocked.
- Added a `containers` section to `commands.json` (read and write paths). The guard blocks the write paths, and a unit test checks that `allow.json` has a rule for every read path.
- The test that every allow pattern starts with a lowercase letter now also accepts `VBoxManage`.

**Still asking:** `ip rule`, `ip -s link`, `docker exec`/`attach`/`compose`, `vagrant status`, virsh on other connection URIs, and a few tools outside this scope (`bash --version`, `column`, `git cat-file`, `tree-sitter --version`).

2. **The `2>&1` form of exact rules.** opencode matches `herdr --help 2>&1` together with its redirection, so the exact rule doesn't fire.

   - Recommendation: a fixed list of harmless variables (`LC_ALL`, `LANG`, `LC_*`, `TZ`, `NO_COLOR`, `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS`, `GIT_PAGER=cat`, `COLUMNS`), only in front of a command that is already allowed.

## Assistant (Build · Claude Opus 5.5 · 47.3s)

_Thinking:_
That `cd ~/GDrive` must come from the tally's recursion into the process substitution, not opencode itself, since opencode doesn't generate cd patterns like that. Also interesting that opencode treats the whole `join ... <(cd ...)` as a single pattern rather than splitting out the process substitution contents separately — I should check what the README says about commands inside process substitutions.

Actually, the echo command in this log isn't listed in patterns at all, which contradicts my assumption that patterns include every simple command. This makes more sense if "always"-approved commands are process-wide: once `echo *` got approved earlier, it stops appearing in later prompts' pattern lists. So patterns only show stages not already covered by rules or prior always-grants, which fits what the brief described.

For the design note, the core evidence is that opencode doesn't generate permission patterns for `cd`, bare variable assignments, `export`, or compound shell keywords like for/if/while/do/done.

It does generate patterns for simple builtin commands like `shift`, `read`, `continue`, `break`, `return`, `true`, `false`, `:`, and `set`. I'm thinking through whether these could be safely globbed — `read` just pulls stdin into a variable so it's not a write risk, and most `set` options like `-e`, `-o pipefail`, or `-x` are harmless since actual redirections get caught separately by the guard anyway.

But `trap` is a real gap: it stores a command string to run later, and I doubt opencode's analyzer looks inside that string, so something like `trap 'rm -rf x' EXIT` wouldn't get flagged even though it's dangerous — that needs to stay a required prompt rather than get globbed, which I should flag as a TODO. Similar concerns apply to `alias`, `source`/`.`, and `builtin`, which can indirectly execute arbitrary code.

I also notice our own decide()/tally reporting diverges from opencode: `cd`, bare assignments, and `export`/`declare` are treated differently because tree-sitter-bash actually parses `export X=1` as a `declaration_command` node, not a plain `command` — that's likely why opencode skips analyzing it. `unset` similarly becomes its own `unset_command` node, and a bare assignment alone becomes `variable_assignments`.

But this raises a real security gap: since opencode never prompts on export/declare nodes, something like `export PATH=/tmp/evil:$PATH; ls` would let a later `ls` silently execute an attacker's binary without triggering any permission check.

So the external diff then runs and actually executes the write, confirming the bypass. My guard only checks for simple `VAR=value` prefixes, not `export VAR=value`, so `export GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=...; git diff` slips through silently while the prefix form without export still triggers a prompt since it doesn't match the allowed "git diff*" pattern. I should also check similar tricks using GIT_PAGER or PAGER with git log.

I'm finding another bypass path: setting GIT_SSH_COMMAND and invoking git ls-remote executes arbitrary commands through the SSH wrapper, which defeats the restriction even without bash access. I'm also noting that unexported shell assignments won't propagate to child processes unless exported explicitly or via `set -a`, but that if the variable happens to already be exported in the environment, the same exploit applies.

I should verify whether opencode actually prompts for "export" commands, since that's the real bypass vector — testing with something like `export GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF='touch /tmp/pwned'; git diff` to see if our decide logic correctly flags it as requiring confirmation, then checking real logs for evidence of how opencode handles export statements.

I wonder if I could verify directly against opencode itself, maybe through debug subcommands, though the integration tests don't actually run bash commands without a real model. It might be worth digging into the compiled binary for traces of how the bash tool parses commands like "cd", searching the embedded JS source for relevant tree-sitter handling.

## Assistant (Build · Claude Opus 5.5 · 88.0s)

_Thinking:_
I'm confirming that opencode walks command nodes in the syntax tree, skipping builtins like cd/pushd, and uses the parent's text when wrapped in a redirected statement. A bare variable assignment isn't itself a command node, but something like `VAR=x cmd` is, since the assignment attaches to the command node.

This points to a real bypass: `export`/`declare`/`unset` are declaration_command nodes, not plain commands, so the analyzer skips them entirely. That means `export GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF='touch x'; git diff` would only flag `git diff`, letting the malicious env var slip through — I want to verify this actually triggers git's external-diff mechanism in a scratch repo. Similarly, test expressions (`[ ]`, `[[ ]]`) parse as test_command rather than command, so they'd also evade detection, while things like `true`, `read`, `exit`, `set` remain plain command nodes and get caught.

I realize `set` is risky too — `set -a` combined with an unprompted assignment could export a variable like GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF that git later executes, so `set` should only be whitelisted for safe flags like -e, -u, -x, -o pipefail, not allexport. `wait` seems fine on its own, but `trap` is dangerous since it executes an arbitrary string as a signal handler.

Now I'm checking decide()/check for divergence from opencode: things like plain `cd`, `pushd`, `popd`, bare variable assignments, and test commands like `[ -f x ]` or `[[ a > b ]]` shouldn't trigger a prompt since opencode treats them as non-command constructs — but my current decide() logic over-flags some of these, which only affects accuracy of the check/CLI tooling, not actual security.

I'm also finding a bigger issue: exported environment variables can hijack otherwise-allowed commands into executing arbitrary code. `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` turns a plain `git diff` into running an external program, and `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`/`GIT_SSH` can redirect `git ls-remote ssh://...` to run a custom SSH command — both are vectors through commands that are normally considered safe.

I'm also noting that `git remote show` runs an ssh command, and pager-related env vars like `GIT_PAGER`/`PAGER` are mostly safe since opencode's bash isn't a tty. But `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS`/`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`KEY_n`/`VALUE_n` let an attacker inject arbitrary git config values—like `core.fsmonitor`, `diff.external`, or `core.sshCommand`—which can trigger code execution through otherwise benign commands like `git status`.

I'm also considering `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` pointing to a malicious repo's config, `LD_PRELOAD`/`LD_LIBRARY_PATH` needing an existing shared library to be useful, `PATH` manipulation needing an existing binary to hijack, `BASH_ENV` only mattering for non-interactive bash invocations, and other pager/editor variables like `LESSOPEN`, `MANPAGER`, `EDITOR`/`VISUAL` that depend on tools not being allowed anyway.

Then I'm checking `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, which could let `rg` execute a `--pre` command if a config file with that directive already exists, though that requires either a pre-existing file or a write capability — an edge case. I rule out other variables like `GREP_OPTIONS`, `TAR_OPTIONS`, `GZIP`, `SYSTEMD_PAGER`, and similar as not applicable here.

I'm now considering `NODE_OPTIONS`, wondering whether node applies it even during `--version`, and realizing `--import` with a `data:` URL could allow injecting arbitrary JavaScript without needing a file on disk, which seems like a promising injection vector through tools like `npm view`.

I'm also checking other environment variables—`PYTHONSTARTUP`, `PYTHONPATH`, `PERL5OPT`, and `mise`-specific variables—to see if any similarly allow code execution during supposedly safe commands, though I'm unsure whether `python3 --version` triggers site customization early enough to matter.

The real bypass pattern I'm converging on is that `export VAR=...;` and `set -a` style assignments are declaration commands that never get flagged, unlike the inline `VAR=x cmd` prefix form which does get prompted. This means already-exported variables like PATH, HOME, LANG, and XDG_* can be reassigned via `VAR=...;` without triggering any prompt, since they're not prefix-form syntax, and this could let an attacker redirect PATH or HOME to influence subsequent command behavior.

Since this PR is meant to be a design note rather than code, I should actually verify one bypass in a harmless sandbox—a scratch repo under /tmp, just touching a test file—to check whether our analyzer actually blocks something like exporting GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF before running git diff. I want to trace through how the command parser handles tokens like "export" and the assignment itself to see if it's correctly flagged.

Tracing through, "export" isn't a keyword, assignment, or wrapper, so it falls through unhandled and returns null, same for the git diff call—meaning this isn't actually blocked, and opencode wouldn't prompt since git diff is allowed and export isn't treated as a command node. I also want to confirm with real git that GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF executes even in non-tty mode, which it does per documentation, so I'll run a quick scratch test to confirm. There's also a related fsmonitor bypass worth checking—git status can trigger a hook command via core.fsmonitor—so I should verify both of these in my isolated sandbox, since they only affect my own harmless scratch repo. This means I need to revise the design note to flag these as real, exploitable bypasses in the current release rather than just theoretical gaps.

Given these are genuine security holes, I should recommend a quick guard fix as its own small PR rather than folding it into 1.4, and flag this clearly in the plan for the orchestrator to decide. Separately, I'm working through how redirection handling interacts with wildcard rules—since the redirected_statement text captures all redirects like `2>&1`, `2>/dev/null`, or output file redirects, I need to figure out whether exact-match rules need explicit twins for common redirect suffixes, or whether a generic wildcard pattern could accidentally let write redirects slip past the guard.

I'm also wondering whether clap's `--help` flag triggers regardless of position, since clap typically short-circuits and prints help the moment it sees `--help` anywhere in the args, before processing the rest.

Given the risk of reasoning about that, it's safer to only add exact-suffix twins like `2>&1` and `2>/dev/null` as generated variants, since those are precise and don't widen the surface. I want to count how many ask-prompts in the log would actually be resolved by stripping those exact trailing redirects before evaluating.

For the env-prefix case, globbing per variable/value combination would explode in complexity, and a wildcard pattern like `LC_ALL=* sort *` is actually dangerous since the `*` could absorb additional env assignments like `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=evil`, letting an attacker smuggle in a different variable entirely.

I'm realizing values need to be literal rather than wildcarded to stay safe, which means enumerating a fixed small set of allowed values (LC_ALL=C, LANG=C, TZ=UTC, etc.) crossed with each allow rule -- roughly thousands of injected rule variants per read-only agent config. I'm weighing whether that's too costly given opencode checks each command against these rules linearly.

Rather than a brute-force expansion, I'm thinking it's better to limit this prefix-stripping to a short list of commonly-prefixed commands (sort, git, ls, date, etc.), or just defer this to a cleaner 2.x hook that normalizes and strips harmless literal env-var prefixes in code before evaluating the rest of the command. For now, my recommendation leans toward either a small generated prefix layer for a fixed command list, or simply waiting for the 2.x solution instead of complicating 1.x further.

The real concern isn't these benign prefixes like `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 git diff` — those don't open any declaration bypass. The actual risk is separate: declaration commands themselves, independent of prefix handling. Also worth noting, `cd` is never prompted on by opencode already, so whether it's "safe to allow" is moot for permission prompts, though it still matters for relative path behavior.

But cd does create a subtler risk — if the agent cds into a directory containing a malicious git repo and then runs something like `git status`, that repo's config could trigger unwanted behavior (e.g. via fsmonitor hooks), regardless of whether cd itself is prompted. Git does have ownership-based `safe.directory` protections, but this is still an edge case worth flagging. Our decide() logic should mirror opencode's approach of skipping cd and assignment-only or declaration-only statements.

I also want to make sure guard handles risky declaration commands: blocking exports or declarations of dangerous variables like PATH, LD_*, GIT_*, NODE_OPTIONS, plus allexport settings, since these could let an attacker smuggle code execution through variable assignment even when the command itself looks benign. The recommendation is for the analyzer to block assignments of a denylist of code-running variables regardless of their position in the command.

A denylist feels like the only workable approach for the guard since an allowlist would create too many false positives on harmless variables, though I recognize a denylist is inherently incomplete. One alternative is to block exports or allexport settings entirely unless every assigned variable is on a small allowlist of genuinely harmless ones like locale or terminal settings, while treating bare non-exported assignments as safe unless they shadow a variable already exported in the environment -- though the guard has no visibility into which variables are actually exported in the shell's runtime environment.

I should keep this note concise. I'm separating which parts can be handled with existing v1 tooling versus what genuinely needs the 2.x hook — things like glob-based builtin allowances and the export/declare/set -a guard can be done now without the hook, since they're just our own tool logic.

For 2>&1 redirection and env prefixes, I can cover a limited, bounded set with exact generated twins today, but a general "strip harmless prefixes/suffixes then evaluate" approach really needs the 2.x hook, since v1's guard can only block patterns, not selectively allow them.

I also want to rerun the before/after counts using evaluate() directly on the raw logged pattern text (matching how opencode actually behaves) rather than relying on decide(), so I'm planning a second tally script that classifies each ask into categories like builtin stages, 2>&1-suffix cases, and env-prefix cases.

To make the divergence concrete, I'll set up a scratch repo exporting GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF with real git, then check our guard's verdict via the CLI — I expect it will say "ask" even though opencode itself wouldn't prompt, which demonstrates the gap clearly enough to write up as a separate fix proposal in the plan.

I should also test a few other edge cases safely in a sandboxed env: GIT_CONFIG_COUNT with fsmonitor via git status, and NODE_OPTIONS using a data: import URL with a simple node --version call, writing any scratch files to /tmp rather than anywhere persistent.

In a scratch repo, each of these ran a command with no prompt:
- `export GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF='touch …'; git diff`
- `export GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=core.fsmonitor GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0='touch …'; git status`
- `export GIT_SSH_COMMAND=…; git ls-remote ssh://…`
- `set -a; GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=…; git diff`

`set -a` itself still prompts today, so that last one only works if `set` gets allowed. Our `check`/`decide()` wrongly reports "ask" for all of these. The `VAR=x cmd` prefix form does prompt, because the prefix is part of the matched text.

**Note content** (PR description, plus `TODO.md` replacing the parked bullets). Counts are stages that still ask in today's log (159 prompts), evaluated on the raw text as opencode sees it:

Builtins that do prompt (shift, read, continue: 4 stages) can get globs now (`shift *`, `continue`, `true`, `:`, `read *`, …). `set` stays exact (`set -e`/`-u`/`-x`/`-o pipefail`), never `set -a`. export interface Analyzer {
```
  /** Decide whether a command line modifies files or system state. */
  analyze(command: string, depth?: number): Verdict
  /** Why a single simple command (already split into words) writes, or null. */
  commandWrites(words: readonly string[], depth?: number): string | null

const analyzers = new WeakMap<Commands, Analyzer>()

/** Build (and cache) an analyzer for a command classification. */
export function createAnalyzer(commands: Commands = loadRules().commands): Analyzer {
  const existing = analyzers.get(commands)
  if (existing) return existing

  const hardWrite = new Set(commands.hardWrite)
  const packageManagers = new Set(commands.packageManagers.names)
  const packageWrite = new Set(commands.packageManagers.writeSubcommands)
  const gitWrite = new Set(commands.git.write)
  const herdrWrite = new Set(commands.herdr.write)
  const containerNames = new Set(commands.containers.names)
  const containerWrite = new Set(commands.containers.write)

  function analyzeCommand(command: string, depth = 0): Verdict {
  const analyzer: Analyzer = { analyze: analyzeCommand, commandWrites }
  analyzers.set(commands, analyzer)
  return analyzer
}

/** Decide whether a command line modifies files or system state, using the shared command classification. */
export function analyze(command: string, commands?: Commands): Verdict {
  return createAnalyzer(commands).analyze(command)
}
```
